title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Identify the spindle's primary mechanical function.
student: What is the primary mechanical function of the rotating shaft or spindle in the industrial assembly?
instructor: The shaft transmits rotational power and torque between machine components while maintaining the required rotational alignment.

title: Source of Mechanical Loading
learningObjectives: Identify the loading transmitted by the shaft.
student: What type of mechanical loading is transmitted through the shaft during operation?
instructor: The shaft carries torque about its longitudinal axis as rotational power is transferred through the machine.

title: Supports and Connections
learningObjectives: Explain the roles of bearings and mounting regions.
student: What roles do the bearing or mounting regions play in the physical shaft assembly?
instructor: They support and align the rotating shaft and constrain its position while allowing the intended rotation. Torque may enter or leave the assembly through a pulley, coupling, tooling interface, or driven component.

title: Torque Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace rotational load transfer through the spindle assembly.
student: Trace the rotational load path through the example shaft assembly.
instructor: Torque enters through the driving component, is transmitted through the shaft, and is transferred to the connected machine or tooling interface.

title: Effect of Changing Shaft Size
learningObjectives: Predict how shaft diameter affects local twist.
student: If different portions of the shaft have different diameters, would you expect them to contribute equally to the total angular twist? Explain qualitatively.
instructor: No. Smaller-diameter regions are less torsionally stiff and therefore contribute more strongly to the total angular twist.

title: Relevant Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Identify responses governing rotational accuracy and strength.
student: What mechanical response is important if angular positioning or rotational accuracy is a design concern?
instructor: The torsional deformation, or angle of twist, is the primary response. Torsional shear stress is also relevant when evaluating the shaft's strength.

title: Relevant Geometric and Material Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify parameters controlling nonprismatic shaft deformation.
student: What geometric, material, and loading characteristics would affect the torsional deformation of a variable-section shaft?
instructor: Relevant characteristics include the applied torque, overall shaft length, variation of shaft radius or diameter along its length, and the material shear modulus.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Convert the industrial spindle into a nonprismatic shaft model.
student: Replace the detailed industrial spindle geometry with an equivalent one-dimensional solid circular shaft whose radius varies continuously along its length. Show the applied torque, restrained end, axial coordinate, and variable radius.
instructor: A correct model shows a solid circular nonprismatic shaft carrying torque about its longitudinal axis. One end is restrained against rotation, the opposite end receives the applied torque, and the shaft radius is represented as a function of axial position.
gradingNotes: The student model should be created before the instructor reference diagram is shown whenever the activity is used to assess representational competence.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting the equivalent spindle model.
student: State the assumptions used to convert the physical spindle into the simplified torsion model.
instructor: Reasonable assumptions are: solid circular shaft; homogeneous isotropic linear-elastic material; Saint-Venant torsion; small rotation; torque acts about the shaft axis; constant shear modulus; continuously varying radius; rigid rotational restraint at one end; and bending, axial loading, local shoulder stress concentrations, bearing flexibility, fatigue, and warping effects are neglected.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the nonprismatic torsion analysis.
student: Before performing numerical calculations, describe the sequence required to determine shaft twist and stress.
instructor: Determine the torsional reaction and internal torque, define the variable polar moment of inertia, write the differential twist relation, integrate along the shaft length, calculate the maximum shear stress, compare the twist with the serviceability limit, and make a mechanics-based recommendation.

title: Boundary Condition and Reaction Torque
learningObjectives: Apply rotational boundary conditions and torque equilibrium.
student: From the instructor reference model, state the rotational boundary condition at the restrained end and determine the reaction torque.
instructor: The restrained-end rotation is zero. Static torque equilibrium requires a reaction torque equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the applied torque: TR = -T. Its magnitude is {{taper_reaction_Nm}} N·m.

title: Internal Torque
learningObjectives: Determine the internal torque function.
student: Determine the internal torque carried by the shaft as a function of position.
instructor: Because there are no additional applied torques along the shaft, the internal torque magnitude is constant: Tint(x) = T for 0 ≤ x ≤ L.

title: Variable Polar Moment of Inertia
learningObjectives: Express polar moment as a position-dependent property.
student: Write the polar moment of inertia as a function of axial position.
instructor: For a solid circular section, J(x) = πr(x)4/2.

title: Differential Twist Relation
learningObjectives: Derive the local rotation relation for a variable-radius shaft.
student: Write the differential relation for shaft rotation.
instructor: Using dφ = Tintdx/[GJ(x)] and Tint = T, dφ = 2Tdx/[πG r(x)4].

title: Angle-of-Twist Integral
learningObjectives: Formulate total twist for the assigned radius profile.
student: Formulate the definite integral for the rotation of the torque-input end relative to the restrained end.
instructor: φ = ∫0L2T/[πG r(x)4]dx, where r(x) = {{taper_r_A_m}}[1 + 0.8(x/L)3/2 + 0.4(x/L)5/2] m.

title: Numerical Evaluation of Twist
learningObjectives: Numerically evaluate the nonprismatic shaft twist.
student: Evaluate the angle-of-twist integral using the assigned variables and report the result in radians and degrees.
instructor: Numerical integration gives φ = {{taper_phi_rad}} rad = {{taper_phi_deg}}°. {{taper_twist_assessment}}

title: Maximum Torsional Shear Stress
learningObjectives: Calculate and locate the maximum torsional shear stress.
student: Determine the maximum torsional shear stress and identify where it occurs.
instructor: For a solid circular shaft, τmax(x) = 2T/[πr(x)3]. Since r(x) increases monotonically, the maximum occurs at the smallest-radius end, x = 0. With r(0) = {{taper_r_A_m}} m, τmax = {{taper_tau_max_MPa}} MPa.

title: Compliance Sensitivity
learningObjectives: Explain why the minimum-radius region dominates twist.
student: Explain why the small-radius region contributes disproportionately to the total shaft twist.
instructor: The local twist rate varies as 1/r(x)4. Therefore even a modest reduction in radius causes a large increase in local torsional compliance. The minimum-radius portion can dominate total rotation even though it occupies only part of the shaft.

title: Stiffness-Based Modification
learningObjectives: Recommend a change that directly reduces twist.
student: The calculated twist exceeds the allowable value. Identify one geometry or material change that would most directly reduce the twist and explain why.
instructor: Increasing the minimum radius near the torque-input end is the most direct geometric change because torsional rigidity scales with r4. Increasing the shear modulus by selecting a stiffer material or shortening the compliant region would also reduce twist.

title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Judge serviceability and recommend a bounded design change.
student: State whether the simplified shaft satisfies the rotational serviceability requirement and provide a concise mechanics-based recommendation.
instructor: {{taper_recommendation}}
gradingNotes: The recommendation should distinguish the governing stiffness criterion from the comparatively low calculated torsional stress and acknowledge the simplified model.
